strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reusing time-series pretraining across forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection. Combining granularity-conditioned modules with autoregressive blank infilling is a plausible design.

Experiments cover three tasks and multiple established datasets. The strongest results are on imputation: average ETTh1 MSE improves from GPT4TS's 0.069 to 0.053, and ETTm1 MSE improves from 0.028 to 0.021.

Comparisons against training from scratch support benefits from pretraining, and forecasting ablations provide initial evidence that the proposed architectural components improve performance. The appendix supplies several useful implementation details.
weaknesses: The central empirical finding does not establish a novel property of universal representations. Changing the sampling interval necessarily changes the frequency axis and Nyquist limit in Hz, while density magnitudes depend on coordinate scaling. Figures 1 and 3 also compare heterogeneous datasets, confounding granularity with domain and signal characteristics. Controlled resampling experiments, normalized-frequency comparisons, and quantitative distribution tests are needed.

The connection between the proposed Fourier block and physical time-series frequencies is unclear. Equation 2 transforms each embedded patch across its learned feature coordinates; the 385-dimensional matrices in Appendix A.2.3 are consistent with transforming the 768-dimensional hidden representation. These coordinates do not retain a defined temporal sampling interval. Moreover, FFT–linear mapping–inverse FFT is itself a linear mapping, so a capacity-matched granularity-conditioned feature-space baseline is necessary to substantiate the claimed frequency-specific advantage.

The claim of adaptation without architectural changes is insufficiently specified. Pretraining uses patches of length 96 and an embedding matrix with 96 input dimensions, whereas imputation explicitly removes patching. The paper does not explain how the same input and output projections remain compatible with scalar tokens. It also leaves unclear how continuous START/END targets are trained and interpreted during generation.

Evaluation does not convincingly establish competitiveness among foundation models. Forecasting comparisons largely reuse published results while GTM dynamically selects context lengths from 96 to 1440, without documenting a matched selection protocol. Timer, a particularly relevant comparator using UTSD, is absent; comparisons with other major forecasting foundation models and unified imputation models are limited. Fine-tuned benchmark performance alone also provides weak support for universal representation claims without zero-shot or held-out-granularity evaluation.

Ablations do not isolate the contributions adequately. There is no comparison of blank infilling against causal forecasting and masked reconstruction under matched data and compute, nor a direct granularity-embedding baseline. Architectural ablations cover only forecasting. Multiple seeds and uncertainty estimates are absent, despite several small gains.

Anomaly detection uses segment-level point adjustment: detecting one point credits the entire anomalous segment. This can substantially inflate F1 and does not demonstrate accurate pointwise detection. Unadjusted or event-based metrics and a clearly specified threshold-selection procedure are needed, particularly because the average advantage over GPT4TS is only about 0.29 F1 percentage points.

Numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evidence. Table 16's ETTh1 MSE values without time granularity average to approximately 0.425, not the reported 0.414; its Traffic values without frequency processing average to approximately 0.398, not 0.392. Tables 3 and 13 disagree on the dataset assignment of Informer's imputation results, and Table 13's Weather PatchTST MSE values average to approximately 0.033 rather than 0.060. The same GTM anomaly scores average to 87.16, conflicting with 87.01 in Table 4. These errors affect comparisons and reported improvements.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendix: masking distributions, the tail-masking proportion, detailed fine-tuning schedules, exact pretraining exclusions, and context-selection procedures are not sufficiently documented. Overall, the promising benchmark results do not outweigh the unresolved methodological and evaluation issues.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reusing pretrained time-series representations across forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection. Combining granularity-conditioned modules with autoregressive blank infilling is a plausible approach.

The evaluation covers three tasks, multiple datasets, forecasting horizons, and missingness rates. Reported imputation improvements on ETTh1 and ETTm1 are substantial, and forecasting results are competitive on several datasets.

Pretraining comparisons and component ablations provide some positive evidence: pretraining generally improves downstream performance, and the complete model achieves better average forecasting errors than the ablated variants. The appendix supplies useful architectural and training details.
weaknesses: The central empirical finding does not establish the claimed new principle of universal representation. Figures 1 and 3 compare different datasets at different sampling intervals, confounding granularity with domain and signal characteristics. Changing the sampling interval also changes frequency support in Hz and probability-density scales mechanically. Controlled resampling of the same signals, normalized-frequency comparisons, and quantitative analysis are needed to establish an effect beyond these expected differences.

The connection between the Fourier module and physical frequency is unclear. Equation 2 applies FFT column-wise to learned patch embeddings; the 768-dimensional embedding and 385-dimensional spectral matrices indicate transformation along latent features rather than the original time axis. Those features have no established temporal ordering. Moreover, Equations 2–4 describe a granularity-conditioned linear transformation in a Fourier basis. A matched conditional linear or low-rank adapter baseline is needed to show that spectral processing itself explains the gains.

The claim of adaptation without architectural changes is insufficiently specified. Pretraining uses 96-point patches with an embedding matrix of shape D × 96 and a patch-output projection, whereas imputation reportedly removes patching while reusing the model unchanged. The paper does not explain how point-wise inputs and outputs remain dimensionally compatible. Masking distributions, fine-tuning hyperparameters, and downstream reconstruction procedures are also insufficiently documented.

Comparisons do not convincingly establish superiority over contemporary foundation models. Timer, a particularly relevant baseline for the unified pretraining claim, is absent from the experimental tables; UniTS is evaluated only for forecasting, and UP2ME only for anomaly detection. Relevant task-specific methods discussed in the paper, such as SAITS and modern anomaly detectors, are also missing. Forecasting results are borrowed from prior work while GTM dynamically selects lookback windows between 96 and 1440, without demonstrating matched tuning budgets or comparable protocols.

The ablations do not isolate the main contributions sufficiently. There is no controlled comparison of blank infilling against ordinary autoregressive or masked-reconstruction pretraining, and architectural ablations cover forecasting only. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported despite several small gains. Fine-tuned performance on standard benchmarks, without zero-shot or controlled unseen-granularity evaluation, provides limited evidence for universal representations.

Anomaly detection relies on point-adjusted F1: detecting one point marks an entire ground-truth anomalous segment as detected. This can substantially inflate performance and does not establish accurate localization or timely detection. Threshold selection is unspecified, and unadjusted, event-level, or threshold-independent metrics are absent. GTM wins only two of five datasets in Table 4, with a small reported average advantage over GPT4TS.

Numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evaluation. Tables 3 and 13 swap Informer's Weather and Electricity averages, changing the apparent Electricity ranking. Table 13's PatchTST Weather averages do not match its individual entries. Identical GTM anomaly scores yield different averages in Tables 4 and 8, and Table 6 includes an unrelated forecasting row. Claims of broad superiority also exceed the tables: GTM trails TTM and PatchTST on average Electricity forecasting, and Table 13 places it behind both PatchTST and Informer on Electricity imputation. These issues require correction before the conclusions can be assessed reliably.

strengths: The goal of sharing a pretrained backbone across forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection is relevant. Combining granularity-conditioned modules with autoregressive blank infilling is a plausible approach.
Imputation results are promising: Table 3 reports average MSE reductions over GPT4TS from 0.069 to 0.053 on ETTh1 and from 0.028 to 0.021 on ETTm1.

The evaluation covers multiple datasets, forecasting horizons, and missingness ratios. Comparisons against training from scratch and component ablations provide evidence that pretraining and granularity conditioning improve average performance.
weaknesses: The central empirical finding does not establish a novel property of universal representations. Figures 1 and 3 compare different datasets at different sampling intervals, confounding granularity with domain and signal characteristics. Changing sampling intervals also changes the physical-frequency range by construction. Controlled resampling of the same signals, with comparable normalization and frequency coordinates, is needed to support the claimed interpretation.

The connection between the Fourier module and physical-frequency knowledge is insufficiently justified. Equation 2 applies FFT within each learned patch embedding rather than along the original time axis; the reported 385-dimensional matrices are consistent with transforming the 768 latent features. Frequencies of arbitrary embedding coordinates need not correspond to temporal frequencies. Furthermore, the stated FFT–linear map–inverse FFT operation is a granularity-conditioned linear transformation in another basis. A parameter-matched temporal-domain alternative is needed to establish the benefit of the Fourier construction.

The claim of architecture-preserving transfer is unresolved. Pretraining uses patch length 96 and an input projection of shape D × 96, whereas imputation reportedly removes patching while reusing pretrained settings. The manuscript does not explain how scalar inputs and outputs remain compatible with these projections. Handling learned START/END vectors in the numerical reconstruction loss and generation procedure is also underspecified.

The comparisons do not convincingly establish competitiveness with closely related foundation models. Timer is central to the motivation but absent from the performance tables; UP2ME is evaluated only on three anomaly datasets, and UniTS only on a subset of forecasting datasets. Baseline results are taken from publications or code while GTM dynamically selects lookback lengths between 96 and 1440, without demonstrating matched tuning budgets and protocols.

Ablations do not test the claimed advantage of unified blank-infilling pretraining over standard autoregressive or masked-reconstruction objectives. Component ablations cover forecasting only, with no parameter-matched conditioning controls or evaluation on held-out granularities. Task-specific fine-tuning results alone provide limited evidence for the broader claim of universal knowledge representation.

Anomaly detection relies exclusively on point-adjusted F1, which credits an entire anomalous segment after one detected point and can substantially inflate performance. Threshold selection is unclear, and unadjusted or event-based metrics are absent. The average improvement over GPT4TS is only 0.29 percentage points in Table 4, with no repeated-run uncertainty; Table 8 also reports an inconsistent GTM average of 87.15 for the same per-dataset scores.

The superiority claims exceed the results: GTM trails TTMs on average forecasting MSE for ETTh1 and Electricity, trails PatchTST on Electricity imputation, and wins only two of five anomaly datasets. Missing seed variability, detailed fine-tuning configurations, masking parameters, and an auditable pretraining-data exclusion list further limit confidence and reproducibility.

strengths: The goal of a reusable time-series model spanning forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification is relevant. Conditioning representations on sampling granularity is a potentially useful design choice.

The evaluation is broad: it includes supervised, zero-shot, and few-shot forecasting, multiple downstream tasks, additional PV and L2C datasets, and comparisons with recent models such as Sundial and Time-MOE.

There are meaningful positive results, particularly on ETT imputation and long-horizon L2C forecasting. The TSB-AD evaluation is a valuable addition beyond point-adjusted anomaly detection, with strong reported performance across several metrics.

The paper provides architecture ablations, comparisons against training from scratch, hyperparameter studies, efficiency measurements, and ten-run confidence intervals for selected forecasting experiments.
weaknesses: The central frequency-domain interpretation is insufficiently established. Appendix B.2.3 specifies 385-dimensional frequency matrices for a 768-dimensional embedding, suggesting an FFT over latent features rather than temporal samples. The relationship between these latent frequencies and the physical-frequency distributions in Figure 1 is unexplained. Moreover, Equations 2–4 describe linear Fourier-domain transformations, which compose into a granularity-conditioned linear operator. A parameter-matched time-domain conditional layer is needed to isolate the benefit of Fourier processing from additional capacity and metadata conditioning.

The claimed novel, task-agnostic pretraining framework is not adequately validated. Span infilling, shuffling, and 2D positional encoding are explicitly adapted from GLM, while the experiments do not separately ablate tail masking, the reconstruction/autoregressive mixture, span shuffling, or positional encoding. Consequently, the evidence does not establish which elements enable cross-task transfer or support the strong 'first generative-task-agnostic' claim.

The downstream implementation is internally unclear. The main text describes autoregressive output generation, whereas Appendix B.3.8 says the implementation generates outputs in parallel and truncates them to the desired horizon. Section 3.4 also permits removing masking and 2D positional encoding, and imputation omits patching despite pretraining with 96-point patches. The paper does not explain how input/output dimensions and pretrained weights remain compatible. These ambiguities obstruct reproduction and assessment of the no-task-specific-modifications claim.

Comparison fairness is insufficiently documented. Many baseline results are imported from papers, while GTM dynamically selects lookback windows between 96 and 1440; matched context lengths and tuning budgets are not established. Details of downstream optimization, zero-shot configurations, anomaly thresholds, and TSB-AD adaptation are incomplete. The code-availability statement has no link. These omissions matter because many forecasting gains are small.

Several quantitative inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results. Table 22 gives Weather PatchTST MSE values averaging approximately 0.033, but reports 0.060; its Informer Weather/Electricity results conflict with Table 2. Table 8 reports a GTM average F1 of 87.15, although its entries average 87.01. Table 20's best counts include dataset-average rows alongside individual horizons, overstating the number of distinct wins. Table 19's repeated-run estimates also differ materially from headline results in some settings, without explaining how the headline runs were selected.

The conclusions exceed the evidence. GTM does not consistently outperform strong baselines: Time-MOE beats it throughout ETTh1 forecasting, and PatchTST/TTM remain competitive or better on Electricity. The main anomaly-detection advantage is small and relies on point adjustment, although TSB-AD partly addresses this concern. Scaling claims are based on limited downstream trends without fitted scaling relationships or compute controls. Finally, calling Fourier attention's overhead marginal is inconsistent with Table 10, where it accounts for roughly three quarters of total inference latency.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: developing a pretrained time-series model that transfers across forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification with limited architectural adaptation.

There are meaningful empirical gains, particularly for imputation on ETTh1 and ETTm1. The appendix strengthens the evaluation with recent forecasting baselines, PV and L2C datasets, and TSB-AD-U results using metrics beyond point-adjusted F1.

The experiments include comparisons with training from scratch, frequency-module ablations, hyperparameter studies, efficiency measurements, and repeated forecasting trials. These provide useful evidence that pretraining and granularity conditioning can improve performance.
weaknesses: The central Fourier mechanism is insufficiently justified. Appendix B.2.3 specifies 385-dimensional frequency matrices for a 768-dimensional embedding, suggesting an FFT over learned embedding coordinates rather than physical time. The connection to the physical-frequency distributions in Figure 1 is therefore unclear. Moreover, Equations 2–4 describe linear transformations around FFT/iFFT; without additional constraints or nonlinearities, this can be represented as a granularity-conditioned linear transformation in the original basis. A parameter-matched conditional linear-layer baseline is needed to establish the specific value of Fourier processing.

The novelty and effectiveness of the pretraining framework are not adequately isolated. Span infilling, span permutation, 2D positional encoding, and mixed attention closely follow the cited GLM framework. The paper does not ablate random-only versus tail-only versus hybrid masking, span shuffling, or 2D positional encoding. Consequently, the experiments do not establish that the proposed combination is responsible for improved transfer across tasks.

The claim of adaptation without task-specific modifications is not convincingly demonstrated. Section 3.4 permits removing masking and 2D positional encoding, while imputation removes patching despite pretraining with 96-point input/output patches. How the pretrained embedding and projection weights remain compatible is unexplained. Additionally, the main text describes autoregressive output generation, whereas Appendix B.3.8 describes parallel sequence output followed by truncation. This unresolved distinction affects reproducibility and interpretation of the efficiency results.

Comparative evaluation does not sufficiently control experimental conditions. Most main-table baseline results are taken from other papers, while GTM dynamically selects lookback lengths up to 1440; matching context lengths, tuning budgets, and checkpoint settings is not established. The additional recent baselines help, but several gains are small or mixed: Time-MOE outperforms GTM on every ETTh1 horizon in Table 20, and TimesFM substantially outperforms GTM on zero-shot ETTm1. The evidence supports competitiveness on selected settings rather than consistent state-of-the-art superiority.

There are substantive reporting inconsistencies. Table 22 gives Weather PatchTST MSE values averaging approximately 0.033, but reports 0.060. Informer’s Weather and Electricity averages are reversed between Tables 2 and 22. Table 8 repeats the five GTM anomaly scores from Table 3 but changes their average from 87.01 to 87.15. Several headline forecasting results also fall outside the corresponding confidence intervals in Table 19 without an explanation of how the main-table runs were selected. These issues reduce confidence in the reported rankings.

The principal anomaly-detection results use point adjustment, which can substantially inflate F1. The TSB-AD-U evaluation is a valuable mitigation, but its dataset coverage, threshold selection, adaptation protocol, and baseline execution details are insufficiently specified. Likewise, the claimed exclusion of downstream data from pretraining is not supported by a dataset-level exclusion list, and the announced code link is absent.

Several broader conclusions exceed the evidence. Figure 1 does not disentangle sampling-rate effects and domain differences from genuinely useful granularity-specific structure. The scaling experiments demonstrate limited empirical trends rather than established scaling laws. The claim that Fourier attention adds only marginal overhead is also inconsistent with Table 10, where it accounts for 0.033 of 0.043 seconds per univariate inference.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: learning reusable time-series representations that support forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, and classification within a largely shared architecture.

Granularity-conditioned low-rank modules provide a plausible mechanism for incorporating sampling metadata. Forecasting ablations across five datasets consistently favor the complete model over versions without granularity conditioning or frequency processing.

The evaluation is broad, including zero-shot and few-shot forecasting, pre-training ablations, additional PV and L2C datasets, and comparisons with Time-MOE and Sundial. Imputation gains on ETT and long-horizon forecasting gains on L2C are particularly promising.

The extended TSB-AD evaluation is valuable: it supplements point-adjusted anomaly scores with multiple metrics and reports improvements on eight of nine measures. Ten-run forecasting confidence intervals and computational measurements are also useful additions.
weaknesses: The central frequency-domain interpretation is insufficiently established. Appendix B.2.3 specifies 385-dimensional spectral matrices for a 768-dimensional embedding, suggesting an FFT over learned feature coordinates rather than physical time. The connection to the physical-frequency distributions in Figure 1 is therefore unclear. Moreover, Equations 2–4 describe linear spectral processing, which can be represented as a granularity-conditioned linear operator in the original coordinates. A parameter-matched time-domain alternative is needed to establish the benefit of the Fourier parameterization.

The proposed pre-training framework lacks the ablations necessary to support a main contribution. Span infilling, shuffled reconstruction, and two-dimensional positional encoding closely follow the acknowledged GLM design. Experiments do not isolate tail masking, span shuffling, positional encoding, or reconstruction-only versus forecasting-only objectives. Consequently, the evidence does not establish which adaptations are necessary or whether the hybrid objective improves transfer.

The claim of adaptation without task-specific modifications is overstated and operationally unclear. Section 3.4 removes masking and two-dimensional positional encoding, while imputation removes patching despite pre-training with 96-point patches. How the pretrained input and output projections accommodate this change is unspecified. Appendix B.3.8 also describes parallel sequence output followed by truncation, whereas the main method repeatedly describes autoregressive generation. The precise training-to-inference transition needs clarification.

Several numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evaluation. Tables 2 and 22 interchange the Weather and Electricity average Informer results. Table 22 reports Weather PatchTST averages of 0.060 MSE and 0.144 MAE, although its individual entries average approximately 0.033 and 0.056. Tables 3 and 8 report different GTM anomaly averages for identical per-dataset scores. Table 20 includes average rows in its win counts, effectively counting the same evidence twice.

Comparative superiority is less convincing than claimed. Many baseline results are imported from other papers while GTM dynamically selects look-back lengths, without a sufficiently documented matched tuning protocol. TTM and PatchTST outperform GTM on several aggregate forecasting metrics; Time-MOE clearly wins on ETTh1; and zero-shot GTM substantially trails TimesFM on ETTm1. Imputation lacks direct comparisons with the closest multitask foundation models. These results support competitiveness on selected settings, rather than consistent state-of-the-art performance.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete. The promised code URL is absent, fine-tuning and model-selection details are limited, and the asserted exclusion of downstream data from pre-training is not documented with a dataset-level manifest. Confidence intervals cover only three forecasting datasets and omit baseline variability; some headline results lie outside the corresponding intervals. These gaps matter because several reported improvements are small.
